case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Kaci May v. Dorchester School District Two
key_cases.citation: Op. No. 6053 (S.C. Ct. App. filed May 29, 2024) (App. Case No. 2020-001352)
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of an injunction, holding S.C. Code § 63-7-920(C) authorizes DSS to interview children at school without a warrant and outside the parents' presence during a mandated investigation, and that the interviews here were reasonable in inception and scope under the Fourth Amendment.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the investigative powers that attach once a report is accepted under § 63-7-920(A)(1).
key_cases.quote: we find § 63-7-920(C) expressly authorizes DSS to interview children at school without a warrant when conducting an investigation mandated by § 63-7-920(A)(1)

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the county, holding the social worker's and deputies' consented entry into the home was reasonable and that medical examinations of the children did not violate the plaintiff's Fourth Amendment rights.
key_cases.relevance: Once a screen is escalated to investigation, Wildauer sets the reduced Fourth Amendment scrutiny that applies to the caseworker's home visit.
key_cases.quote: investigative home visits by social workers are not subject to the same scrutiny as searches in the criminal context

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Wilson
key_cases.holding: The court held that a parent facing an intervention petition and entry on the Central Registry has a protected liberty interest and a due process right of confrontation, and that allowing the child to testify outside his presence without an individualized finding of trauma violated that right.
key_cases.relevance: Wilson describes the statutory path from investigation to an intervention petition and the preponderance finding that must precede any registry entry.
key_cases.quote: Because Wilson did not have the opportunity to be heard in a meaningful manner, his due process right was violated.

key_cases.case_name: South Carolina Department of Social Services v. Randy S.
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals of South Carolina
key_cases.holding: The court held that where DSS in substance removed children and placed them with a relative, it had brought a removal action and was required to follow the removal procedures — petition, 72-hour probable cause hearing, 35-day merits hearing — rather than proceeding as an intervention.
key_cases.relevance: It describes the 24-hour preliminary investigation DSS must conduct to decide whether emergency custody was proper and whether removal can be avoided.
key_cases.quote: Despite DSS's contention that this was only an intervention action, we find the evidence supports a finding that Children were removed from Father's custody.

key_cases.case_name: Renn ex rel. Renn v. Garrison
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit vacated the denial of qualified immunity, holding the social services defendants acted within the authority state statute gave them to investigate reported neglect and that their conduct stayed inside the clearly established boundaries of the family privacy right.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that the State's legitimate interest in curtailing abuse of its minor citizens justifies extending an investigation beyond the four corners of the original complaint once other indicators of neglect appear.
key_cases.quote: we find as well that their actions were reasonable under the circumstances in relation to the boundaries of the family privacy right that had been clearly established

mandatory_reporters: Listed professionals only, acting in their professional capacity (South Carolina is not a universal-reporter state) — S.C. Code Ann. § 63-7-310(A)
Physicians, nurses, dentists, optometrists, medical examiners, coroners, and employees of a county medical examiner's or coroner's office
Any other medical, emergency medical services, mental health, or allied health professional
Members of the clergy, including Christian Science practitioners and religious healers
Clerical or nonclerical religious counselors who charge for services
School teachers, counselors, principals, assistant principals, and school attendance officers
Childcare workers in a childcare center or foster care facility
Undertakers, funeral home directors, and employees of a funeral home
Volunteer non-attorney guardians ad litem serving on behalf of the South Carolina Guardian ad Litem Program or Richland County CASA
Any other person may report and is encouraged to report — S.C. Code Ann. § 63-7-310(D)

other: Encourages, condones, or approves the commission of delinquent acts by the child and those acts are shown to be the result of the encouragement, condonation, or approval
